# A new approach to principal–agent problems with volatility control

**Authors:** Alessandro Chiusolo ††thanks: Department of Operations Research and Financial Engineering (ORFE), Princeton University, NJ 08544. Research partially supported by the NSF grant DMS-2307736. Emma Hubert11footnotemark: 1

## Abstract

The recent work by Cvitanić, Possamaï, and Touzi (2018) [9] presents a general approach for continuous-time principal–agent problems, through dynamic programming and second-order backward stochastic differential equations (BSDEs). In this paper, we provide an alternative formulation of the principal–agent problem, which can be solved simply by relying on the theory of BSDEs. This reformulation is strongly inspired by an important remark in [9], namely that if the principal observes the output process $X$ in continuous-time, she can compute its quadratic variation pathwise. While in [9], this information is used in the contract, our reformulation consists in assuming that the principal could directly control this process, in a ‘first-best’ fashion. The resolution approach for this alternative problem actually follows the line of the so-called ‘Sannikov’s trick’ in the literature on continuous-time principal–agent problems, as originally introduced by Sannikov (2008) [29]. We then show that the solution to this ‘first-best’ formulation is identical to the solution of the original problem. More precisely, using the contract form introduced in [9] as penalisation contracts, we highlight that this ‘first-best’ scenario can be achieved even if the principal cannot directly control the quadratic variation. Nevertheless, we do not have to rely on the theory of 2BSDEs to prove that such contracts are optimal, as their optimality is ensured by showing that the ‘first-best’ scenario is achieved. We believe that this more straightforward approach to solve continuous-time principal–agent problems with volatility control will facilitate the dissemination of these problems across many fields, and its extension to even more intricate problems.

Keywords. Principal–agent problems, volatility control, moral hazard, first-best, BSDEs.

AMS 2020 subject classifications. Primary: 91B43; secondary: 91B41, 93E20.

## 1 Introduction

Contract theory, and more precisely principal–agent problems, offer a relevant framework for the study of optimal incentives between agents, especially with information asymmetry. In standard principal–agent problems, a principal (she) is imperfectly informed about the actions of an agent (he). To incentivise the agent to act in her best interest, she can offer him a contract, usually represented by a terminal payment $\xi$ at a fixed finite time horizon $T>0$ . The main mathematical challenge of these problems is to determine an optimal contract, in the sense that it maximises the utility of the principal, while that of the agent is held at least to a given level. The design of such a contract raises first of all an issue of information: the contract can only depend on what is known, or observable, by the principal. We focus in this paper on the moral hazard case, i.e. when the effort of the agent is hidden and therefore not contractible.

For a long time, these problems were only considered in discrete-time or static settings, in particular with the works of Mirrlees in [23] (1976) and [24] (1999), or the seminal papers of Holmström (1979) [15] and Grossman and Hart (1983) [12]. However, discrete-time models are actually challenging to solve, especially because the existence of an optimal contract in these settings is more the exception than the rule, even in very simple and natural examples. The theory then regained momentum with the first continuous-time formulation of the problem by Holmström and Milgrom (1987) [16], and later by Sannikov (2008) [29], using tools from stochastic control theory. Through these works, it is established that, if the agent only controls the drift of a stochastic process $X$ , continuously observable by the principal, then the optimal contract $\xi$ should have the following form,

$$ \displaystyle\xi=y_{0}-\int_{0}^{T}{\cal H}(t,X_{t},Z_{t})\mathrm{d}t+\int_{0}^{T}Z_{t}\cdot\mathrm{d}X_{t}, $$

where ${\cal H}$ here is the (simplified) agent’s Hamiltonian for drift control. In the previous contract form, the constant $y_{0}\in\mathbb{R}$ and the process $Z$ have to be optimally chosen by the principal, in order to maximise her utility and ensure the participation of the agent in the contractual agreement. More precisely, the choice of $y_{0}\in\mathbb{R}$ is usually dictated by the agent’s participation constraint, while the process $Z$ will incentivise the agent to perform appropriate effort on the drift of the output process. This form of contract naturally comes from the study of the agent’s continuation utility, which, in the case of drift control only, can be related to the solution of a backward stochastic differential equation (BSDE for short). This formal link between the agent’s continuation utility and the contract itself was introduced by Sannikov (2008) [29], and thus usually referred to as ‘Sannikov’s trick’ in the literature on continuous-time principal–agent problems, but has recently been revisited in a more theoretical way by Possamaï and Touzi (2024) [27]. These problems have subsequently been extended in many directions, for example to consider multi-agent and/or multi-principal problems, a continuum of agents with mean-field interactions, more general output process $X$ , more intricate information asymmetry between the two parties, to only cite a few.

In terms of theoretical developments, the most significant breakthrough is thanks to Cvitanić, Possamaï, and Touzi (2018) [9], who have developed a general and rigorous theory that allows to address a wide spectrum of principal–agent problems, especially when the agent can also control the volatility of the output process. As explained in [9], moral hazard problems in continuous-time in which the agent controls the volatility are notoriously harder to study. Indeed, in this case, his continuation utility cannot be related to the solution of a BSDE anymore, one has to rely now on the theory of backward stochastic differential equations of the second order (2BSDE for short), introduced by Soner, Touzi, and Zhang (2012) [30] and further developed by Possamaï, Tan, and Zhou (2018) [28]. One important observation made in [9] which will also be at the heart of our approach is that, if the principal has access to the trajectory of the output process $X$ , then she can deduce its quadratic variation process $\langle X\rangle$ in a pathwise manner, as demonstrated by Bichteler (1981) [4]. This motivates the authors to introduce a new form of contracts, namely

$$ \displaystyle\xi=y_{0}-\int_{0}^{T}{\cal H}(t,X_{t},Z_{t},\Gamma_{t})\mathrm{d}t+\int_{0}^{T}Z_{t}\cdot\mathrm{d}X_{t}+\dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}{\rm Tr}\big[\Gamma_{t}\mathrm{d}\langle X\rangle_{t}\big]. $$

These contracts are indexed on $X$ as before, but also on its quadratic variation $\langle X\rangle$ through an additional parameter $\Gamma$ , which would incentivise the agent to perform appropriate efforts on the volatility. Note that the agent’s Hamiltonian ${\cal H}$ here should be different from the one introduced in the previous contract form, precisely to take into account volatility control. When restricting the study to this form of contracts, it is straightforward to show, mostly using Ito’s formula, that the agent’s optimal effort will naturally be given by the maximiser of the Hamiltonian. One can then proceed by solving the principal’s optimal control problem, namely by writing the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB for short) equation corresponding to her stochastic control problem, which becomes relatively standard under the restriction to the previous form of contracts. These first two steps are therefore quite straightforward using standard tools from stochastic control theory. However, the third and last step requires to prove that the restriction to such form of contracts is without loss of generality. While the approach provided in [9] to prove this main result relies on the theory of 2BSDEs, the aim of this paper is precisely to present an alternative approach which avoids relying on this sophisticated theory. For the sake of comparison, we will study the same general model, whose original formulation will be recalled in Section 2.

Despite the challenges raised when studying principal–agent problems with volatility control, especially as the optimality of revealing contracts relies on deep results from the recent theory of 2BSDEs, it has subsequently been extended and applied in many different situations. We can mention in a non-exhaustive way the applications related to finance by the same authors in [8], by Cvitanić and Xing (2018) [7] or more recently by Baldacci and Possamaï (2022) [3]; the works by Aïd, Possamaï, and Touzi (2022) [1], Élie, Hubert, Mastrolia, and Possamaï (2021) [11] and Aïd, Kemper, and Touzi (2023) [2] for applications related to the energy sector; as well as other various extensions, e.g., the works of Mastrolia and Possamaï (2018) [22], Hernández Santibáñez and Mastrolia (2019) [14], Hu, Ren, and Touzi (2019) [17], Hubert (2023) [18] or Keppo, Touzi, and Zuo (2024) [21]. Naturally, the study of applications fitting into the general framework proposed in [9] can be done in a fairly straightforward way, directly using the results, as done in [8, 1]. Nevertheless, the recent research mentioned above has also attempted to generalise principal–agent problems, especially to consider many agents (see [18, 2]), or even a continuum (see [11]). If one follows the approach developed in [9], these extensions require to introduce the so-called multidimensional or mean-field 2BSDEs, and study, or assume, the well-posedness of such systems. However, while the theory on (one-dimensional) 2BSDEs is sufficiently developed to address relatively general principal–agent problems, there is currently no definition nor existence results on multidimensional/mean-field 2BSDEs. This further motivates the presentation in this paper of an alternative approach. We believe that this novel approach, which avoids relying on the theory of 2BSDEs, will greatly facilitate the study of relevant generalised principal–agent problems, especially with many agents, or non-continuous output processes.

Before introducing the approach developed in this paper, we wish to provide more intuition on the problem under consideration via a short detour through the so-called first-best case. When studying principal–agent problems with moral hazard, it is quite common to compare the results with this benchmark scenario, in which the principal can directly optimise the agent’s effort. This problem is usually easier to solve, as one only has to consider the principal’s stochastic control problem under the agent’s participation constraint. It may happen in the moral-hazard case, sometimes also referred to as second-best, that the principal can actually deduce, through her observation, the effective efforts of the agent. In this scenario, the two problems, first-best and second-best, are then equivalent if the principal can design a contract which strongly penalises the agent whenever he deviates from the optimal effort recommended by the principal. Typically, the principal will offer to the agent a minimal11 1 Minimal in the sense that it would just be sufficient to ensure the participation of agent. compensation if he follows the recommendation, and threaten him with a high penalty if he deviates from it. These forcing contracts can usually be implemented if no strong assumptions are made on the admissible contract’s form.

As highlighted before, the approach developed by Cvitanić, Possamaï, and Touzi (2018) [9] relies in particular on the observation that, if the principal have access to the trajectory of the output process $X$ , she can actually compute its quadratic variation $\langle X\rangle$ pathwise, and thus design contracts of the form (2.11), indexed on $X$ and $\langle X\rangle$ through sensitivity parameters $Z$ and $\Gamma$ to be optimised. The main idea behind our reformulation of the original principal–agent problem with volatility control is that, since the principal can deduce the quadratic variation $\langle X\rangle$ , she could probably force the agent to choose his efforts in order to achieve an optimal quadratic variation. In other words, the idea here is to study an alternative ‘first-best’ formulation of the original problem, in which the principal enforces a contract $\xi$ as well as a quadratic variation process. The agent should then optimise his effort in order to maximise his expected utility given such contract $\xi$ as before, but now the admissible set of efforts is restricted to those achieving the quadratic variation imposed by the principal.

When considering the agent’s problem in this ‘first-best’ alternative formulation, described with more details in Section 3.1, one can remark that, since the quadratic variation is a priori fixed by the principal, the agent’s weak formulation boils down to choosing equivalent probability measures by means of Girsanov theorem. For a fixed quadratic variation process and any contract $\xi$ , the agent’s continuation utility can therefore be represented by means of a BSDE, instead of a 2BSDE in the original formulation. More informally, one can actually apply the so-called ‘Sannikov’s trick’ to obtain a relevant representation of the contract $\xi$ , which is then similar to the optimal form of contracts in principal–agent problems with drift control only, namely (1.1). Following this straightforward approach, we establish in Section 3.2 that the principal’s problem boils down to a more standard stochastic control problem, in the sense that she should maximise her expected utility by optimally choosing the contract’s parameters, namely a constant $y_{0}\in\mathbb{R}$ and an appropriate process $Z$ , as well as the quadratic variation process.

However, as mentioned before, the moral-hazard case is equivalent to its first-best counterpart if the principal can deduce the agent’s control from her observations and design a forcing contract. Indeed, even if the principal observes the agent’s control, she may not have enough bargaining power to actually force the agent to perform the optimal efforts. Similarly, in our problem, even if the principal observes the quadratic variation of the output process, she may not be able to actually force the agent to follow the recommended quadratic variation. Therefore, to ensure the equivalence between the original problem and its ‘first-best’ reformulation, we need to introduce appropriate forcing contracts, which allow the principal to achieve her ‘first-best’ utility even if she cannot directly control the quadratic variation. It is already quite clear that the contracts introduced in [9] will perfectly serve this purpose. Indeed, as these contracts are optimal when the principal observes the quadratic variation, they should allow her to achieve the expected utility she would have if she could directly control the quadratic variation process. We thus use in Section 3.3 the contract form (1.2) to conclude that the principal’s value in the reformulated problem coincides with the one derived in [9]. In other words, from the principal’s point of view, optimising over $\Gamma$ in the contract form (1.2) or directly optimising over admissible quadratic variation lead to the exact same results. In particular, this result confirms that the contracts introduced in [9] are also optimal when the agent’s efforts on the volatility can actually be determined by the principal through her observation of the quadratic variation. Interestingly, our approach further reveals the importance of an additional assumption under which the contract form (1.2) is indeed optimal and the above equivalence holds. Specifically, if Assumption B is not satisfied, the method of [9] may fail to yield optimal contracts, as explained in Remark 3.12 and illustrated through a counter-example in Section 4.3.

To summarise, this paper provides an alternative yet more accessible approach to solve principal–agent problems with volatility control, in particular to prove that the contract form introduced in [9] is without loss of generality from the principal’s point of view. More precisely, we first solve a ‘first-best’ reformulation of the original problem by means of the theory of BSDEs, and then show that the contract form introduced in [9] allows to achieve this first-best scenario, and is therefore naturally optimal. We believe that this simpler approach will enable better dissemination of these problems in various fields across mathematical finance, economics, management sciences, operation research; fostering their use in many relevant applications. Furthermore, as this new approach only relies on the theory of BSDEs, we believe that it will facilitate the study of relevant extensions of principal–agent problems, for example when considering such a Stackelberg game with many agents, as well as its mean-field limit, when the principal can contract with a continuum of agents. We nevertheless emphasise that our approach relies on Assumption A, which is not assumed in [9]. More precisely, to apply the BSDE theory without introducing an orthogonal martingale component, we require a martingale representation theorem to hold; Assumption A provides a sufficient condition for this. We refer the reader to Remarks 2.2 and 3.3 for a more detailed discussion. While this assumption appears necessary for our current arguments, we believe it constitutes a relatively mild condition, especially given the significant simplification afforded by our approach. Extending the method beyond the scope of Assumption A remains an open question, but we believe there is good reason to expect that such generalisations are possible and would preserve the validity of our main results.

The structure of the paper is as follows. We first introduce in Section 2 the continuous-time principal–agent problem considered by Cvitanić, Possamaï, and Touzi (2018) [9]. We also briefly describe the main steps of the approach they developed to solve the problem, highlighting the main challenges posed by this approach. Section 3 details the main results of this paper: we first introduce in Section 3.1 the alternative ‘first-best’ reformulation of the original principal–agent problem, we then characterise in Section 3.2 the optimal form of contracts, relying only on the theory of BSDEs, and we finally prove in Section 3.3 that the solution of the reformulated problem coincides with the solution of the original problem. To further highlight the link between the two formulations, we provide in Section 4 some illustrative examples in which the solution can be explicitly characterised. Finally, Section 5 concludes by providing further related research directions.

#### Notations.

Let $\mathbb{N}^{\star}:=\mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\}$ be the set of positive integers, and recall that $T>0$ denotes some maturity fixed in the contract. For any $(\ell,c)\in\mathbb{N}^{\star}\times\mathbb{N}^{\star}$ , $\mathbb{M}^{\ell,c}$ will denote the space of $\ell\times c$ matrices with real entries. When $\ell=c$ , we let $\mathbb{M}^{\ell}:=\mathbb{M}^{\ell,\ell}$ , and denote by $\mathbb{S}_{+}^{\ell}$ the set of $\ell\times\ell$ non-negative definite (or positive semi-definite) symmetric matrices with real entries. For any $d\in\mathbb{N}^{\star}$ , let ${\cal C}([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{d})$ denote the set of continuous functions from $[0,T]$ to $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . The set ${\cal C}([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{d})$ will always be endowed with the topology associated to the uniform convergence on the compact $[0,T]$ . For a probability space of the form $\Omega:={\cal C}([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{d})$ and an associated filtration $\mathbb{F}$ , we will have to consider processes $\psi:[0,T]\times{\cal C}([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{k})\longrightarrow E$ , taking values in some Polish space $E$ , which are $\mathbb{F}$ -optional, i.e. ${\cal O}(\mathbb{F})$ -measurable where ${\cal O}(\mathbb{F})$ is the so-called optional $\sigma$ -field generated by $\mathbb{F}$ -adapted right-continuous processes. In particular, such a process $\psi$ is non-anticipative in the sense that $\psi(t,x)=\psi(t,x_{\cdot\wedge t})$ , for all $t\in[0,T]$ and $x\in{\cal C}([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{k})$ . Furthermore, for any filtration $\mathbb{F}:=({\cal F}_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}$ and probability measure $\mathbb{P}$ , we will denote by:

- $\bullet$ $\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{P}}:=({\cal F}_{t}^{\mathbb{P}})_{t\in[0,T]}$ the usual $\mathbb{P}$ -completion of $\mathbb{F}$ ;

- $\bullet$ $\mathbb{F}^{+}:=({\cal F}_{t}^{+})_{t\in[0,T]}$ the right limit of $\mathbb{F}$ ;

- $\bullet$ $\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{P}^{+}}:=({\cal F}_{t}^{\mathbb{P}^{+}})_{t\in[0,T]}$ the augmentation of $\mathbb{F}$ under $\mathbb{P}$ .

Finally, for technical reasons, we work under the classical ZFC set-theoretic axiom. This is a standard axiom widely used in the classical stochastic analysis theory (see Dellacherie and Meyer (1978) [10, Chapter 0.9]). We also rely on the continuum hypothesis, which is needed to apply the aggregation result of Nutz (2012) [26].

## 2 General model

In order to highlight that our alternative approach to principal–agent problems with volatility control allows to obtain the same results as in [9], we focus here on the exact same model. We believe that this model is sufficiently general to convince the reader of the relevance of our novel approach, and that it could then be extended in a (relatively) straightforward way to solve more complex problems.

We fix throughout this paper a finite time horizon $T>0$ , and consider the canonical space $\Omega={\cal C}([0,T];\mathbb{R}^{d})$ , $d\in\mathbb{N}^{\star}$ . The output process $X$ controlled by the agent is originally defined as the canonical process on $\Omega$ , i.e.

$$ \displaystyle X_{t}(x)=x(t),\quad\text{for all }\;x\in\Omega,\;t\in[0,T]. $$

We denote by $\mathbb{F}=({\cal F}_{t})_{t\geq 0}$ its canonical filtration, defined for all $t\in[0,T]$ by ${\cal F}_{t}=\sigma(X_{s},s\in[0,t])$ . Let ${\cal M}$ be the set of all probability measures on $(\Omega,{\cal F}_{T})$ , and define ${\cal M}_{\rm loc}$ the subset of ${\cal M}$ such that, for each $\mathbb{P}\in{\cal M}_{\rm loc}$ , $X$ is a $(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{F})$ –local martingale whose quadratic variation, denoted $\langle X\rangle$ , is absolutely continuous in time with respect to the Lebesgue measure. Using the result by Karandikar (1995) [20], the quadratic variation process $\langle X\rangle$ can be defined pathwise, in the sense that there exists an $\mathbb{F}$ –progressively measurable process which coincides with the quadratic variation of $X$ , $\mathbb{P}$ –a.s. for any $\mathbb{P}\in{\cal M}_{\rm loc}$ . Moreover, we can introduce the corresponding $\mathbb{F}$ –progressively measurable density process $\widehat{\sigma}^{2}$ , defined by

$$ \displaystyle\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{t}:=\limsup_{\varepsilon\searrow 0}\dfrac{\langle X\rangle_{t}-\langle X\rangle_{t-\varepsilon}}{\varepsilon},\quad t\in[0,T]. $$

For all $t\in[0,T]$ , $\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{t}\in\mathbb{S}_{+}^{d}$ , recalling that $\mathbb{S}_{+}^{d}$ denotes the set of $d\times d$ positive semi-definite symmetric matrices with real entries. We can thus define the corresponding square root process, simply denoted $\widehat{\sigma}$ , in the usual way.

### 2.1 Controlled output process

To represent the agent’s controls on the drift and the volatility of the output process $X$ , we let $U$ be a finite-dimensional Euclidean set and consider the following coefficients:

$$ \displaystyle\lambda:[0,T]\times\Omega\times U\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n},\quad\text{and}\quad\sigma:[0,T]\times\Omega\times U\longrightarrow\mathbb{M}^{d,n}. $$

As in [9], we assume that both coefficients are bounded, and that the mappings $\lambda(\cdot,u)$ and $\sigma(\cdot,u)$ are $\mathbb{F}$ -optional for any $u\in U$ . In particular, recall that such mappings are non-anticipative, in the sense that $\lambda(t,x,u)=\lambda(t,x_{\cdot\wedge t},u)$ and $\sigma(t,x,u)=\sigma(t,x_{\cdot\wedge t},u)$ , for all $t\in[0,T]$ and $x\in\Omega:={\cal C}([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{d})$ . We will rigorously define later the set ${\cal U}$ of admissible controls, namely appropriate processes taking values in $U$ , and consider, for all $\nu\in{\cal U}$ , the following stochastic differential equation (SDE for short), driven by an $n$ -dimensional Brownian motion $W$ , for $n\in\mathbb{N}^{\star}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}X_{t}=\sigma(t,X,\nu_{t})\big(\lambda(t,X,\nu_{t})\mathrm{d}t+\mathrm{d}W_{t}\big),\;t\in[0,T]. $$

To rigorously introduce the weak formulation for the agent’s problem, one may need to enlarge the original canonical space by considering

$$ \widebar{\Omega}:=\Omega\times{\cal C}([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{n})\times\mathbb{U}, $$

where $\mathbb{U}$ is the collection of all finite and positive Borel measures on $[0,T]\times U$ , whose projection on $[0,T]$ is the Lebesgue measure. In other words, every $q\in\mathbb{\mathbb{U}}$ can be disintegrated as $q(\mathrm{d}t,\mathrm{d}u)=q_{t}(\mathrm{d}u)\mathrm{d}t$ , for an appropriate Borel measurable kernel $q_{t}$ , $t\in[0,T]$ . The weak formulation requires to consider a subset of $\mathbb{U}$ , namely the set $\mathbb{U}_{0}$ of all $q\in\mathbb{U}$ such that the kernel $q_{t}$ is of the form $\delta_{\phi_{t}}(\mathrm{d}u)$ for some Borel function $\phi$ , where as usual, $\delta_{\phi_{t}}$ is the Dirac mass at $\phi_{t}$ , $t\in[0,T]$ . This space is supporting a canonical process $(X,W,\Pi)$ defined by:

$$ \displaystyle X_{t}(x,\omega,q) \displaystyle:=x(t),\;W_{t}(x,\omega,q):=\omega(t),\;\Pi(x,\omega,q):=q,\;(t,x,\omega,q)\in[0,T]\times\widebar{\Omega}. $$

Then, the canonical filtration $\widebar{\mathbb{F}}:=(\widebar{\cal F}_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}$ is defined as the following $\sigma$ -algebra,

$$ \displaystyle\widebar{\cal F}_{t}:=\sigma\Big(\big(X_{s},W_{s},\Delta_{s}(\varphi)\big)\text{ s.t. }(s,\varphi)\in[0,t]\times{\cal C}_{b}\big([0,T]\times U,\mathbb{R}\big)\Big),\;t\in[0,T], $$

where ${\cal C}_{b}([0,T]\times U,\mathbb{R})$ is the set of all bounded continuous functions from $[0,T]\times U$ to $\mathbb{R}$ , and

$$ \displaystyle\Delta_{s}(\varphi):=\int_{0}^{s}\int_{U}\varphi(r,u)\Pi(\mathrm{d}r,\mathrm{d}u),\text{ for any }\;(s,\varphi)\in[0,T]\times{\cal C}_{b}([0,T]\times U,\mathbb{R}). $$

Finally, let ${\cal C}^{2}_{b}(\mathbb{R}^{k},\mathbb{R})$ for any $k\in\mathbb{N}^{\star}$ denotes the set of bounded twice continuously differentiable functions from $\mathbb{R}^{k}$ to $\mathbb{R}$ , whose first and second derivatives are also bounded. For any $(t,\psi)\in[0,T]\times{\cal C}^{2}_{b}(\mathbb{R}^{d+n},\mathbb{R})$ , we set

$$ \displaystyle M_{t}(\psi):=\psi(X_{t},W_{t})-\int_{0}^{t}\int_{U}\bigg( \displaystyle\ \widebar{\Lambda}(s,X,u)\cdot\nabla\psi(X_{s},W_{s})+\frac{1}{2}{\rm Tr}\Big[\nabla^{2}\psi(X_{s},W_{s})\big[\widebar{\Sigma}\widebar{\Sigma}^{\top}\big](s,X,u)\Big]\bigg)\Pi(\mathrm{d}s,\mathrm{d}u), $$

where $\nabla\psi$ and $\nabla^{2}\psi$ denote the gradient vector and the Hessian matrix of $\psi$ , respectively, and where $\widebar{\Lambda}$ and $\widebar{\Sigma}$ are respectively the drift vector and the diffusion matrix of the $(d+n)$ -dimensional vector process $(X,W)^{\top}$ , i.e.

$$ \displaystyle\widebar{\Lambda}(s,x,u):=\begin{pmatrix}[\sigma\lambda](s,x,u)\\
\mathbf{0}_{n}\end{pmatrix},\;\widebar{\Sigma}(s,x,u):=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{0}_{d,d}&\sigma(s,x,u)\\
\mathbf{0}_{n,d}&\mathrm{I}_{n}\\
\end{pmatrix},\;s\in[0,T],\;x\in\Omega,\;u\in U. $$

Let $\widebar{\cal M}$ be the set of all probability measures on $(\widebar{\Omega},\widebar{\cal F}_{T})$ . We fix some initial conditions, namely $x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ representing the initial value of $X$ , and define the following subset of $\widebar{\cal M}$ .

#### Definition 2.1.

The subset $\widebar{\cal P}\subset\widebar{\cal M}$ is composed of all $\widebar{\mathbb{P}}$ such that

- $(i)$ $M(\psi)$ is a $(\widebar{\mathbb{P}},\widebar{\mathbb{F}})$ -local martingale on $[0,T]$ for all $\psi\in{\cal C}^{2}_{b}(\mathbb{R}^{d+n},\mathbb{R});$

- $(ii)$ there exists some $w_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ such that $\widebar{\mathbb{P}}[(X_{0},W_{0})=(x_{0},w_{0})]=1;$

- $(iii)$ $\widebar{\mathbb{P}}\big[\Pi\in\mathbb{U}_{0}]=1$ .

Using the classical result by Stroock and Varadhan (1997) [31, Theorem 4.5.2] in our already enlarged canonical space, one can rigorously define the required dynamics for $X$ under $\mathbb{P}\in\widebar{\cal P}$ . In particular, we have that, for all $\mathbb{P}\in\widebar{\cal P}$ , there exists some $\widebar{\mathbb{F}}$ -predictable process $\nu:=(\nu_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}$ , taking values in $U$ , such that $\Pi(\mathrm{d}s,\mathrm{d}u)=\delta_{\nu_{s}}(\mathrm{d}u)\mathrm{d}s$ $\mathbb{P}$ –a.s., and we obtain the desired representation for $X$ , namely

$$ \displaystyle X_{t}=x_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}\sigma(s,X,\nu_{s})\big(\lambda(s,X,\nu_{s})\mathrm{d}s+\mathrm{d}W_{s}\big),\;t\in[0,T],\;\mathbb{P}\textnormal{--a.s.} $$

With this in mind, for any $\mathbb{P}\in\widebar{\cal P}$ , we denote by $\widebar{\cal U}(\mathbb{P})$ the set of $\widebar{\mathbb{F}}$ -predictable and $U$ -valued processes $\nu$ such that (2.3) holds, and consider

$$ \displaystyle\widebar{\cal U}:=\bigcup_{\mathbb{P}\in\widebar{\cal P}}\widebar{\cal U}(\mathbb{P}), $$

as well as for any $\nu\in\widebar{\cal U}$ , the set of corresponding probability measures $\widebar{\cal P}(\nu):=\{\mathbb{P}\in\widebar{\cal P}:\nu\in\widebar{\cal U}(\mathbb{P})\}$ . Finally, to avoid technical considerations (see Remark 2.2 below), we make the following standing assumption.

#### Assumption A.

Each agent’s admissible controls induce a unique weak solution to SDE (2.3), i.e. $\nu\in{\cal U}$ with

$$ \displaystyle{\cal U}:=\big\{\nu\in\widebar{\cal U}:\widebar{\cal P}(\nu)\;\text{is a singleton}\;\{\mathbb{P}^{\nu}\}\big\}. $$

We thus have a one-to-one correspondence between any admissible control $\nu\in{\cal U}$ and a probability measure $\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}$ , where ${\cal P}$ is defined accordingly:

$$ \displaystyle{\cal P}:=\bigcup_{\nu\in{\cal U}}\widebar{\cal P}(\nu). $$

In the following, we will alternatively refer to the unique probability measure in ${\cal P}$ associated with an admissible control $\nu\in{\cal U}$ as $\mathbb{P}^{\nu}$ , or the unique admissible control in ${\cal U}$ associated with a probability measure $\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}$ as $\nu^{\mathbb{P}}$ .

#### Remark 2.2.

Assumption A is not enforced in [9], but is considered here to avoid technical considerations regarding the martingale representation property. We refer to Remark 3.3 for further discussions on this point, but wish to justify here that this assumption is not far-fetched. Indeed, it is relatively common in the study of principal–agent problems to at least assume that the martingale representation is valid (see Hernández Santibáñez (2024) [13, Assumption 2.2. and Remark 2.3] for example), and weak uniqueness for SDE (2.3) is a sufficient and more explicit condition for such representation to hold. Furthermore, as one of the main objectives of principal–agent problems is to determine ‘revealing’ contracts, i.e. contracts that reveal the agent’s optimal efforts, it is actually questionable to consider efforts that would induce several weak solutions for SDE (2.3), especially in view of applications.

### 2.2 The original principal–agent problem

As usual in principal–agent problems, the principal first chooses a contract $\xi$ , which represents the compensation paid to the agent at the final time horizon $T$ . Naturally, this contract can only be indexed on what is observable by the principal, and should incentivise the agent to appropriately choose a control $\nu\in{\cal U}$ , or equivalently a probability $\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}$ . Here, the principal only observes the output process $X$ , and therefore any admissible contract $\xi$ should be ${\cal F}_{T}$ -measurable, recalling that $\mathbb{F}:=({\cal F}_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}$ represents the canonical filtration of $X$ .

#### The agent’s problem.

Given a compensation $\xi$ , the optimisation problem faced by the agent is defined by

$$ \displaystyle V_{\rm A}(\xi):=\sup_{\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}}J_{\rm A}(\xi,\mathbb{P}),\;\text{ with }\;J_{\rm A}(\xi,\mathbb{P}):=\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}\bigg[{\cal K}_{\rm A}^{\mathbb{P}}(T)\,\xi-\int_{0}^{T}{\cal K}_{\rm A}^{\mathbb{P}}(s)c_{\rm A}\big(s,X,\nu_{s}^{\mathbb{P}}\big)\mathrm{d}s\bigg],\quad\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}, $$

where

- $(i)$ the measurable cost function $c_{\rm A}:[0,T]\times{\cal C}([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{d})\times U\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is such that for any $u\in U$ , the map $(t,x)\longmapsto c_{\rm A}(t,x,u)$ is $\mathbb{F}$ -optional, and satisfies the following integrability condition: $\displaystyle\sup_{\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}\bigg[\int_{0}^{T}\big|c_{\rm A}\big(t,X,\nu^{\mathbb{P}}_{t}\big)\big|^{p}\mathrm{d}t\bigg]<+\infty,\;\text{for some }p>1;$ (2.6)

- $(ii)$ the discount factor ${\cal K}_{\rm A}^{\mathbb{P}}$ is defined for all $\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}$ by

$$ {\cal K}_{\rm A}^{\mathbb{P}}(t):=\exp\bigg(-\int_{0}^{t}k_{\rm A}\big(s,X,\nu_{s}^{\mathbb{P}}\big)\mathrm{d}s\bigg),\quad t\in[0,T], $$

where $k_{\rm A}:[0,T]\times{\cal C}([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{d})\times U\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is assumed to be measurable, bounded, and such that for any $u\in U$ , the map $(t,x)\longmapsto k_{\rm A}(t,x,u)$ is $\mathbb{F}$ -optional.

To ensure that the agent’s problem (2.5) is well-defined, we require minimal integrability on the contracts as in [9, Equation (2.5)], namely

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}\big[|\xi|^{p}\big]<+\infty,\;\text{ for some }\;p>1. {\rm I}^{p}_{\rm A} $$

In addition, we assume as usual that the agent has a reservation utility level $R_{\rm A}\in\mathbb{R}$ , which conditions his acceptance of the contract. We thus denote by $\Xi$ the set of admissible contracts:

$$ \displaystyle\Xi:=\big\{{\cal F}_{T}\text{-measurable random variable $\xi$, satisfying \eqref{eq:integrability_contract_agent} and}\;V_{\rm A}(\xi)\geq R_{\rm A}\big\}. $$

Finally, we denote by ${\cal P}^{\star}(\xi)$ the set of optimal responses of the agent to a contract $\xi\in\Xi$ , i.e.

$$ \displaystyle{\cal P}^{\star}(\xi):=\big\{\mathbb{P}^{\star}\in{\cal P}\;\text{such that}\;V_{\rm A}(\xi)=J_{\rm A}(\xi,\mathbb{P}^{\star})\big\}. $$

#### Remark 2.3.

As mentioned in [9, Remark 2.1], the model and the approach can be extended in a straightforward way to account for risk-aversion in the agent’s utility function. More precisely, in the agent’s expected utility (2.5), $\xi$ can be replaced by $U_{\rm A}(\xi)$ for an appropriate utility function $U_{\rm A}$ , modulo the modification of the integrability condition ( I p A ). As we choose to follow the model considered in [9], we do not consider any utility functions here, but we will nevertheless informally address a case of CARA utility functions through the examples in Section 4.

#### The principal’s problem.

The principal’s optimisation problem is then defined as follows,

$$ \displaystyle V_{\rm P}:=\sup_{\xi\in\Xi}\sup_{\mathbb{P}^{\star}\in{\cal P}^{\star}(\xi)}J_{\rm P}(\xi,\mathbb{P}^{\star}),\;\text{ with }\;J_{\rm P}(\xi,\mathbb{P}):=\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}\Big[{\cal K}_{\rm P}(T)\,U_{\rm P}\big(\ell(X)-\xi\big)\Big],\quad(\xi,\mathbb{P})\in\Xi\times{\cal P}, $$

where

- $(i)$ $U_{\rm P}:\mathbb{R}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is a non-decreasing and concave utility function;

- $(ii)$ $\ell:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is a liquidation function with linear growth;

- $(iii)$ the discount factor ${\cal K}_{\rm P}$ is defined as follows, with $k_{\rm P}:[0,T]\times\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}$ measurable, bounded and $\mathbb{F}$ -optional,

$$ {\cal K}_{\rm P}(t):=\exp\bigg(-\int_{0}^{t}k_{\rm P}(s,X)\mathrm{d}s\bigg),\quad 0\leq t\leq s\leq T. $$

Through (2.9), we implicitly assume as in [9] that, if the agent’s optimal response to a given contract $\xi$ is not unique, then the principal is able to choose the most appropriate one. On the contrary, if a contract $\xi\in\Xi$ is such that ${\cal P}^{\star}(\xi)=\varnothing$ , then by convention of the supremum, the corresponding expected utility for the principal would be $-\infty$ . We can thus assume without loss of generality that any relevant contract $\xi\in\Xi$ should ensure that there exists at least an optimal response $\mathbb{P}^{\star}\in{\cal P}^{\star}(\xi)$ , i.e. ${\cal P}^{\star}(\xi)\neq\varnothing$ .

For future reference, we summarise this original problem below.

#### Problem 1 (Original principal–agent problem).

Consider the non-standard stochastic control problem (2.9),

$$ \displaystyle V_{\rm P}:=\sup_{\xi\in\Xi}\sup_{\mathbb{P}^{\star}\in{\cal P}^{\star}(\xi)}J_{\rm P}(\xi,\mathbb{P}^{\star}),\;\text{ with }\;{\cal P}^{\star}(\xi)\neq\varnothing\;\text{ for }\;\xi\in\Xi. $$

Usually, Problem 1 cannot be solved directly: the standard approach is to determine an appropriate form of contracts which simplifies both the agent’s and the principal’s problems, and such that the restriction to this form of contracts is without loss of generality.

Note that the previous setting and assumptions are relatively standard in continuous-time principal–agent problems, and in particular coincide with the framework described in [9]. Indeed, as the goal of this paper is to provide a new approach to solve such principal–agent problems, which in particular requires to show that this approach allows to achieve the same results obtained by Cvitanić, Possamaï, and Touzi (2018) [9], the decision was made to closely follow their original framework. It is nevertheless possible that some assumptions could be relaxed, or at least modified to consider alternative frameworks. For example, in the case of a principal–agent problem with non-continuous output processes (and many agents), one can refer to the recent paper by Hernández Santibáñez (2024) [13] for more general assumptions. It should be noted, however, that the latter focuses on control processes that can be represented through equivalent changes of measures, thus a priori excluding volatility control.

### 2.3 The existing approach, via 2BSDEs

In this section, we describe briefly and rather informally the general approach developed by Cvitanić, Possamaï, and Touzi (2018) [9], as this will help in comparing it with our new approach, detailed later in Section 3.

#### Revealing contracts.

The general approach developed in [9] involves first identifying a class of contracts, offered by the principal, that are revealing, in the sense that the agent’s optimal response to the contract can easily be computed. With this in mind, we first define the appropriate agent’s Hamiltonian,

$$ \displaystyle{\cal H}_{\rm A}(t,x,y,z,\gamma) \displaystyle:=\sup_{u\in U}\;h_{\rm A}(t,x,y,z,\gamma,u), \displaystyle\text{ with }\;h_{\rm A}(t,x,y,z,\gamma,u) \displaystyle:=[\sigma\lambda](t,x,u)\cdot z+\dfrac{1}{2}{\rm Tr}\big[\gamma[\sigma\sigma^{\top}](t,x,u)\big]-c_{\rm A}(t,x,u)-k_{\rm A}(t,x,u)y,\quad u\in U, $$

for any $(t,x,y,z,\gamma)\in[0,T]\times\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{M}^{d}$ . We then introduce the relevant form of contracts, namely $\xi=Y_{T}^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma}$ , where the process $Y^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma}$ is defined as the solution to the following SDE,

$$ \displaystyle Y_{t}^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma}=y_{0}-\int_{0}^{t}{\cal H}_{\rm A}\big(s,X,Y^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma}_{s},Z_{s},\Gamma_{s}\big)\mathrm{d}s+\int_{0}^{t}Z_{s}\cdot\mathrm{d}X_{s}+\dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{t}{\rm Tr}\big[\Gamma_{s}\mathrm{d}\langle X\rangle_{s}\big],\quad\mathbb{P}\textnormal{--a.s.},\;\text{for all }\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}, $$

for a constant $y_{0}\in\mathbb{R}$ and a pair $(Z,\Gamma)$ of processes satisfying appropriate integrability conditions. More precisely, for any $\mathbb{F}$ -predictable $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ -valued process $Z$ and any $\mathbb{F}$ -optional $\mathbb{R}$ -valued process $Y$ , we consider the following norms,

$$ \displaystyle\|Z\|^{p}_{\mathbb{H}^{p}}:=\sup_{\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}\Bigg[\bigg(\int_{0}^{T}Z_{t}^{\top}\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{t}Z_{t}\mathrm{d}t\bigg)^{p/2}\Bigg],\;\text{ and }\;\|Y\|^{p}_{\mathbb{D}^{p}}:=\sup_{\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}\bigg[\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\big|Y_{t}\big|^{p}\bigg]. $$

We can then define the set ${\cal V}$ of appropriate processes $(Z,\Gamma)$ as in [9, Definition 3.2], recalled below.

#### Definition 2.4.

Let $y_{0}\in\mathbb{R}$ . For any $\mathbb{F}$ -predictable processes $(Z,\Gamma)$ taking values in $\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{M}^{d}$ , define the process $Y^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma}$ using (2.11). We will denote $(Z,\Gamma)\in{\cal V}$ if moreover

- $(i)$ $\|Z\|^{p}_{\mathbb{H}^{p}}<\infty$ and $\|Y^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma}\|^{p}_{\mathbb{D}^{p}}<\infty$ for some $p>1$ ;

- $(ii)$ there exists $\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}$ such that $\displaystyle{\cal H}_{\rm A}\big(t,X,Y_{t}^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma},Z_{t},\Gamma_{t}\big)=h_{\rm A}\big(t,X,Y_{t}^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma},Z_{t},\Gamma_{t},\nu^{\mathbb{P}}_{t}\big),\quad\mathrm{d}t\otimes\mathbb{P}\text{--a.e. on }[0,T]\times\Omega.$

Then, the relevant contracts $\xi\in\Xi$ are those that admit the representation $\xi=Y_{T}^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma}$ , where the pair $(Z,\Gamma)\in{\cal V}$ as well as the constant $y_{0}\in\mathbb{R}$ in (2.11) will be optimally chosen by the principal.

#### Agent’s optimal response.

Contracts of the form (2.11) are called revealing, as it is straightforward to prove that any agent’s best response to such contracts corresponds to a maximiser of his Hamiltonian. Indeed, relying on Ito’s formula, it is proved in [9, Proposition 3.3] that, given a contract of the form $\xi=Y_{T}^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma}$ , $(y_{0},Z,\Gamma)\in\mathbb{R}\times{\cal V}$ , any optimal response $\mathbb{P}^{\star}\in{\cal P}^{\star}(\xi)$ is such that

$$ \displaystyle{\cal H}_{\rm A}\big(t,X,Y_{t}^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma},Z_{t},\Gamma_{t}\big)=h_{\rm A}\big(t,X,Y_{t}^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma},Z_{t},\Gamma_{t},\nu^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}}_{t}\big),\quad\mathrm{d}t\otimes\mathbb{P}^{\star}\textnormal{--a.e. on }[0,T]\times\Omega. $$

For later use, we can define, through a classical measurable selection argument, the following function $u^{\star}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle u^{\star}(t,x,y,z,\gamma)\in\argmax_{u\in U}h_{\rm A}(t,x,y,z,\gamma,u),\;(t,x,y,z,\gamma)\in[0,T]\times\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{M}^{d}, $$

so that the agent’s best response to a contract $\xi=Y_{T}^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma}$ can be written as $\nu^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}}_{t}:=u^{\star}(t,X,Y_{t}^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma},Z_{t},\Gamma_{t})$ , $t\in[0,T]$ , $\mathbb{P}^{\star}$ –a.s. One can also prove that the value of the agent’s optimal control problem associated to such contract $\xi$ of the form (2.11) boils down to $y_{0}$ , namely $V_{\rm A}(Y_{T}^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma})=y_{0}$ . Consequently, to ensure the agent’s participation in the contractual agreement, it is clear that the principal must choose $y_{0}\geq R_{\rm A}$ .

#### Principal’s problem.

Under the restriction to contracts of the form (2.11), the principal’s problem boils down to a more standard stochastic control problem of the following form:

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{V}_{\rm P}:=\sup_{y_{0}\geq R_{\rm A}}\underline{V}_{\rm P}(y_{0}),\;\text{ with }\;\underline{V}_{\rm P}(y_{0}):=\sup_{(Z,\Gamma)\in{\cal V}}\sup_{\mathbb{P}^{\star}\in{\cal P}^{\star}(Y_{T}^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma})}J_{\rm P}\big(Y_{T}^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma},\mathbb{P}^{\star}\big). $$

In particular, for fixed $y_{0}\geq R_{\rm A}$ , the value $\underline{V}_{\rm P}(y_{0})$ corresponds to the value of a stochastic control problem with two state variables, $X$ and $Y^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma}$ . Notice that, under $\mathbb{P}^{\star}\in{\cal P}^{\star}(Y_{T}^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma})$ , the process $X$ admits the following dynamics,

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}X_{t}=\sigma\big(t,X,\nu^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}}_{t}\big)\Big(\lambda\big(t,X,\nu_{t}^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}}\big)\mathrm{d}t+\mathrm{d}W_{t}\Big),\quad t\in[0,T], $$

corresponding to [9, Equation (3.6)]. Using this dynamics for $X$ under the optimal effort, one can also compute the dynamics satisfied by the process $Y^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma}$ defined in (2.11) to obtain for all $t\in[0,T]$

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}Y_{t}^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma}= \displaystyle\ \bigg(Z_{t}\cdot[\sigma\lambda]\big(t,X,\nu_{t}^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}}\big)+\dfrac{1}{2}{\rm Tr}\Big[\Gamma_{t}\big[\sigma\sigma^{\top}\big]\big(t,X,\nu_{t}^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}}\big)\Big]-{\cal H}_{\rm A}\big(t,X,Y^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma}_{t},Z_{t},\Gamma_{t}\big)\bigg)\mathrm{d}t+Z_{t}\cdot\sigma\big(t,X,\nu_{t}^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}}\big)\mathrm{d}W_{t}, $$

similarly to [9, Equation (3.8)]. Using the definition of the Hamiltonian as well as the fact that the optimal effort is defined as one of its maximiser, we can actually further simplify the previous dynamics to obtain,

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}Y_{t}^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma}= \displaystyle\ \Big(c_{\rm A}\big(t,X,\nu_{t}^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}}\big)+Y_{t}^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma}k_{\rm A}\big(t,X,\nu_{t}^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}}\big)\Big)\mathrm{d}t+Z_{t}\cdot\sigma\big(t,X,\nu_{t}^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}}\big)\mathrm{d}W_{t},\quad t\in[0,T]. $$

Again for future reference, it would be convenient to summarise this restricted problem as follows.

#### Problem 2 (Restriction to contracts of the form (2.11)).

Consider the standard stochastic control problem (2.14),

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{V}_{\rm P}:=\sup_{y_{0}\geq R_{\rm A}}\underline{V}_{\rm P}(y_{0}),\;\text{ with }\;\underline{V}_{\rm P}(y_{0}):=\sup_{(Z,\Gamma)\in{\cal V}}\sup_{\mathbb{P}^{\star}\in{\cal P}^{\star}(Y_{T})}J_{\rm P}\big(Y_{T},\mathbb{P}^{\star}\big). $$

where the state variable $(X,Y)$ is solution to the following system of SDEs:

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}X_{t} \displaystyle=\sigma\big(t,X,\nu^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}}_{t}\big)\Big(\lambda\big(t,X,\nu^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}}_{t}\big)\mathrm{d}t+\mathrm{d}W_{t}\Big),\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\;\;t\in[0,T], \displaystyle\mathrm{d}Y_{t} \displaystyle=\Big(c_{\rm A}\big(t,X,\nu^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}}_{t}\big)+Y_{t}\,k_{\rm A}\big(t,X,\nu^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}}_{t}\big)\Big)\mathrm{d}t+Z_{t}\cdot\sigma\big(t,X,\nu^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}}_{t}\big)\mathrm{d}W_{t},\quad t\in[0,T], $$

coupled through the agent’s optimal effort $\nu^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}}_{t}:=u^{\star}(t,X,Y_{t},Z_{t},\Gamma_{t})$ under $\mathbb{P}^{\star}\in{\cal P}^{\star}(Y_{T})$ .

In a Markovian setting, one can solve this stochastic control problem as usual, namely by writing the principal’s Hamiltonian as well as the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB for short) equation satisfied by the value function $\underline{V}_{\rm P}(y_{0})$ (see [9, Theorem 3.9]), and finally optimise it over $y_{0}\geq R_{\rm A}$ . More importantly for our purpose in this paper, one can already remark that the value of Problem 2 should be lower than the value in Problem 1, since considering contracts $\xi$ of the form (2.11) is a restriction of the original set $\Xi$ of admissible contracts. This result can be found in [9, Proposition 3.4], and is a direct consequence of [9, Proposition 3.3] mentioned above. For further reference, this result is stated in the lemma below.

#### Lemma 2.5.

The original value defined by Problem 1 is greater than the value in Problem 2, namely $V_{\rm P}\geq\widetilde{V}_{\rm P}$ .

#### Optimality of the revealing contracts.

To summarise, when restricting the study to contracts $\xi\in\Xi$ of the form (2.11), one can first easily determine the agent’s optimal response to such contract, namely by computing the maximiser of his Hamiltonian. Then, still under this restriction, the principal’s problem boils down to a more standard stochastic problem, namely Problem 2. These two steps are therefore quite straightforward using standard tools from stochastic control theory. However, the last and crucial step requires to prove that the restriction to revealing contracts is without loss of generality. More precisely, one need to argue that the value of the original principal’s problem, namely $V_{\rm P}$ recalled in Problem 1, actually coincides with the value when restricting to revealing contracts, i.e. $\widetilde{V}_{\rm P}$ in Problem 2. While it is clear that $V_{\rm P}\geq\widetilde{V}_{\rm P}$ , as mentioned in Lemma 2.5 above, the main mathematical challenge is to show the converse inequality, namely $V_{\rm P}\leq\widetilde{V}_{\rm P}$ . This result, stated in [9, Theorem 3.6], relies on the sophisticated theory of second-order BSDEs. We deliberately omit to further develop this step here, as it is precisely the part that our new approach allows us to bypass. It nevertheless seems essential to stress that this is the most difficult stage, which probably prevents a wider application of principal–agent problems with volatility control, but also hampers natural extensions of these problems, as discussed in introduction. Surprisingly, our approach reveals that if Assumption B is not satisfied, the method in [9] may fail to yield optimal contracts. We refer the reader to Remark 3.12 for a more detailed discussion of this point, and to Section 4.3 for an illustrative example.

## 3 A new approach

In this section, we first start by formalising a ‘first-best’ alternative problem, in which the principal, in addition to offering a contract, also controls the quadratic variation of the output process. We then provide in Section 3.2 a straightforward resolution approach for this alternative problem, relying on the theory of BSDEs only. We will finally prove in Section 3.3 that this reformulation actually leads to the exact same solution compared to the original problem considered in Section 2.

### 3.1 The ‘first-best’ formulation

As already mentioned, the approach developed by Cvitanić, Possamaï, and Touzi (2018) [9] mostly relies on the observation that, if the principal has access to the trajectory of $X$ , she can actually compute its quadratic variation $\langle X\rangle$ pathwise. In general, observing the quadratic variation would still prevent the principal from deducing the controls on the volatility, hence the relevance of considering contract of the form (2.11), indexed on $X$ and $\langle X\rangle$ through sensitivity parameters $Z$ and $\Gamma$ to be optimised. The main idea behind our reformulation is to assume further that, since the principal can compute the quadratic variation $\langle X\rangle$ , she could actually directly control it. In other words, the idea here is to study an alternative ‘first-best’ formulation of the original principal–agent problem with volatility control, in which the principal enforces a contract $\xi$ as well as a quadratic variation characterised by its density process $\Sigma$ . The agent should then optimise his effort in order to maximise his expected utility given such contract $\xi$ as before, but now the admissible set of efforts is restricted to those achieving the quadratic variation imposed by the principal. More precisely, we will consider in the reformulated problem that, given a contract $\xi$ and a quadratic variation density process $\Sigma$ , the agent should optimally choose his effort $\nu$ on the drift and the volatility of the output process $X$ so that $\mathrm{d}\langle X\rangle_{t}=\Sigma_{t}\mathrm{d}t$ for all $t\in[0,T]$ . Then, the principal’s optimisation problem boils down to choosing the optimal contract $\xi$ and the optimal quadratic variation density process $\Sigma$ .

To consider the agent’s problem in this ‘first-best’ reformulation, we shall again fix a contract $\xi$ , but also an appropriate process $\Sigma$ , representing the density of the quadratic variation with respect to the Lebesgue measure. Both would be chosen optimally by the principal, anticipating the agent’s best response. With this in mind, we define the admissible set of processes $\Sigma$ by

$$ \displaystyle{\cal S}:=\big\{\Sigma\;\mathbb{F}\text{--progressively measurable process, taking values in}\;\mathbb{S}^{d}_{+}\}, $$

recalling that $\mathbb{S}_{+}^{d}$ denotes the set of $d\times d$ positive semi-definite symmetric matrices with real entries. For any process $\Sigma\in{\cal S}$ , we will denote by $\Sigma^{1/2}$ its $(d,d)$ -dimensional symmetric square root, and by $\Sigma^{-1/2}$ its pseudo-inverse.

For fixed $\Sigma\in{\cal S}$ , the agent’s admissible efforts are now limited to those that achieve the desired quadratic variation. Mathematically, the set of admissible controls should be modified as follows:

$$ \displaystyle{\cal U}^{\circ}(\Sigma) \displaystyle:=\big\{\nu\in{\cal U}\;:\;\nu_{t}\in U_{t}^{\circ}(X,\Sigma_{t}),\;t\geq 0\}, \displaystyle\text{ with }\;U_{t}^{\circ}(x,S) \displaystyle:=\big\{u\in U\;:\;\big[\sigma\sigma^{\top}\big](t,x,u)=S\big\},\quad(t,x,S)\in[0,T]\times\Omega\times\mathbb{S}^{d}_{+}. $$

Accordingly, the set ${\cal P}^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ of admissible probability measures is defined by:

$$ \displaystyle{\cal P}^{\circ}(\Sigma):=\big\{\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}\;:\;\big[\sigma\sigma^{\top}\big](t,X,\nu_{t}^{\mathbb{P}})=\Sigma_{t},\;\mathbb{P}\text{--a.s.}\}. $$

#### Remark 3.1.

In this framework, as the density of the quadratic variation is fixed to some process $\Sigma\in{\cal S}$ , one can actually write the weak formulation for the agent’s problem by means of Girsanov’s theorem. More precisely, one can originally define the canonical process $X$ through the following SDE,

$$ \displaystyle X_{t}=x_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}\Sigma_{s}^{1/2}\mathrm{d}W^{\circ}_{s},\quad t\in[0,T], $$

where $W^{\circ}$ is a $d$ -dimensional Brownian Motion. We can show that starting from a weak solution $\widebar{\mathbb{P}}\in{\cal P}$ to (3.3), one can construct, for any $\nu\in{\cal U}^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ , a weak solution $\mathbb{P}^{\nu}\in{\cal P}^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ to the original SDE (2.3) through absolute continuous change of measure.

We proceed in two steps. We first relate the previous SDE to the following one:

$$ \displaystyle X_{t}=x_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}\sigma(s,X,\nu_{s})\mathrm{d}W_{s},\quad t\in[0,T], $$

where $W$ is a $n$ -dimensional Brownian Motion. For this, we consider an additional $(n-d)$ -dimensional Brownian Motion $W^{1}$ , potentially defined on an extended probability space, such that $\widebar{W}:=(W^{\circ},W^{1})$ is an $n$ -dimensional Brownian Motion. Moreover, denote by ${\cal R}_{n}$ the set of all matrices of rotations of $\mathbb{M}^{n}$ , i.e. $R\in\mathbb{M}^{n}$ such that $RR^{\top}=I_{n}$ . For any $R\in{\cal R}_{n}$ , we will further denote by $R^{\circ}$ the $(d,n)$ -dimensional matrix consisting of the $d$ first rows of $R$ , and $R^{1}$ the $(n-d,n)$ -dimensional matrix consisting of the $n-d$ remaining rows of $R$ . For a given control process $\nu\in{\cal U}^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ , let $(R_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}$ be an ${\cal R}_{n}$ -valued optional process with

$$ \displaystyle R_{t}^{\circ}:=\Sigma_{t}^{-1/2}\sigma(t,X,\nu_{t}),\quad t\in[0,T], $$

where $\Sigma_{t}^{-1/2}$ denotes the pseudo-inverse of $\Sigma_{t}^{1/2}$ for all $t\in[0,T]$ , and $(R^{1}_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}$ arbitrary. By Levy’s characterisation of Brownian Motion, the process $W$ defined by $\mathrm{d}W_{t}=R_{t}^{\top}\mathrm{d}\widebar{W}_{t}$ for all $t\in[0,T]$ is also a $\widebar{\mathbb{P}}$ –Brownian Motion, and SDE (3.3) can be rewritten as

$$ \displaystyle X_{t}=x_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}\Sigma_{s}^{1/2}\mathrm{d}W^{\circ}_{s}=x_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}\Sigma_{s}^{1/2}R_{s}^{\circ}\mathrm{d}W_{s}=x_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}\sigma(s,X,\nu_{s})\mathrm{d}W_{s},\quad t\in[0,T]. $$

In other words, any weak solution $\widebar{\mathbb{P}}$ to SDE (3.3) is also a weak solution to SDE (3.4). Note that the converse also holds, simply by Levy’s characterisation of Brownian Motion.

Consider then the following exponential local martingale

$$ \displaystyle M^{\nu}_{t}:={\cal E}_{t}\bigg(\int_{0}^{\cdot}\lambda(s,X,\nu_{s})\mathrm{d}W_{s}\bigg),\quad t\in[0,T], $$

where ${\cal E}$ denotes the Doleans–Dade exponential, namely

$$ \displaystyle{\cal E}_{t}(M):=\exp\bigg(M_{t}-\dfrac{1}{2}\langle M\rangle_{t}\bigg),\quad t\in[0,T], $$

for any local martingale $M$ . As $\lambda$ is assumed to be bounded, the process $M^{\nu}$ defined above is actually a martingale, and one can thus apply Girsanov’s theorem. In particular, by defining the following change of probability,

$$ \displaystyle\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}^{\nu}}{\mathrm{d}\widebar{\mathbb{P}}}\bigg|_{{\cal F}_{T}}=M^{\nu}_{T}, $$

the process $W^{\nu}$ defined by

$$ \displaystyle W^{\nu}_{\cdot}:=W_{\cdot}-\int_{0}^{\cdot}\lambda(s,X,\nu_{s})\mathrm{d}s $$

is a $n$ -dimensional $\mathbb{P}^{\nu}$ –Brownian Motion, and $X$ admits the following representation:

$$ \displaystyle X_{t}=x_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}[\sigma\lambda](s,X,\nu_{s})\mathrm{d}s+\int_{0}^{t}\sigma(s,X,\nu_{s})\mathrm{d}W^{\nu}_{s},\quad t\in[0,T]. $$

Therefore, starting from a weak solution $\widebar{\mathbb{P}}$ to (3.4), any admissible control process $\nu\in{\cal U}^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ induces a weak solution $\mathbb{P}^{\nu}\in{\cal P}^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ to SDE (2.3). The converse is also true, simply by inverting the above construction.

Informally, the previous remark highlights that, when the quadratic variation is fixed, then the agent’s impact on the output process $X$ can be defined as equivalent change of measures through Girsanov’s theorem. In other words, for fixed $\Sigma\in{\cal S}$ , the set ${\cal P}^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ is dominated by $\widebar{\mathbb{P}}$ , weak solution to (3.4). Note that $\widebar{\mathbb{P}}$ obviously depends on the original choice of $\Sigma\in{\cal S}$ , but for simplicity we decide to omit this dependency in the notations, especially since $\Sigma\in{\cal S}$ will be fixed to solve the agent problem.

#### Remark 3.2.

The previous remark is also mentioned in [9, Section 4.4]. Indeed, in order to deal with volatility control in the original stochastic control problem for the agent, the idea is to first isolate the control of the quadratic variation, thus considering the following reformulation of the agent’s problem:

$$ \displaystyle V_{\rm A}(\xi)=\sup_{\Sigma\in{\cal S}}\sup_{\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}^{\circ}(\Sigma)}J_{\rm A}(\xi,\mathbb{P}). $$

For fixed $\Sigma\in{\cal S}$ , all probability measures $\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ are equivalent through Girsanov’s theorem, as mentioned in the previous remark. One can therefore represent the value function of the agent for fixed quadratic variation as a backward stochastic differential equation. Then, since the agent can optimise over admissible quadratic variations, his problem becomes a supremum of BSDEs, i.e. a second-order BSDE. While we will follow the exact same first step, namely to represent the agent’s continuation utility as a BSDE, we will not have to deal with the second step as in our ‘first-best’ problem, the quadratic variation is chosen by the principal, not delegated to the agent.

We can finally formalise the principal–agent problem in this ‘first-best’ scenario. More precisely, given a contract $\xi$ and a quadratic variation density process $\Sigma\in{\cal S}$ , the optimisation problem faced by the agent is defined by

$$ \displaystyle V^{\circ}_{\rm A}(\xi,\Sigma):=\sup_{\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}^{\circ}(\Sigma)}J_{\rm A}(\xi,\mathbb{P}). $$

In parallel to (2.7) and (2.8), for fixed $\Sigma\in{\cal S}$ , we define the set $\Xi^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ of admissible contracts as

$$ \displaystyle\Xi^{\circ}(\Sigma):=\big\{{\cal F}_{T}\text{-measurable random variable $\xi$, satisfying \eqref{eq:integrability_contract_agent} and}\;V^{\circ}_{\rm A}(\xi,\Sigma)\geq R_{\rm A}\big\}. $$

and denote by ${\cal P}^{\circ,\star}(\xi,\Sigma)$ the set of agent’s optimal response.

Then, the goal of the principal is to maximise her objective function by choosing the optimal quadratic variation process $\Sigma\in{\cal S}$ as well as the optimal contract $\xi\in\Xi^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ , anticipating the agent’s optimal response:

$$ \displaystyle V_{\rm P}^{\circ}:=\sup_{\Sigma\in{\cal S}}\sup_{\xi\in\Xi^{\circ}(\Sigma)}\sup_{\mathbb{P}^{\star}\in{\cal P}^{\circ,\star}(\xi,\Sigma)}J_{\rm P}(\xi,\mathbb{P}^{\star}). $$

Recall that by convention, the supremum over an empty set is equal to $-\infty$ . In particular, if the principal suggests a quadratic variation which is not implementable by the agent, then the set ${\cal P}^{\circ,\star}(\xi,\Sigma)$ would be empty, leading to a utility of $-\infty$ for the principal, which cannot be optimal. Therefore, we can assume without loss of generality that for any potentially optimal $\Sigma\in{\cal S}$ , there exists an admissible effort $\nu\in{\cal U}^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ , and thus a corresponding probability measure $\mathbb{P}^{\nu}\in{\cal P}^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ , such that for all $t\in[0,T]$ , $\Sigma_{t}=[\sigma\sigma^{\top}](t,X,\nu_{t}),\;\mathbb{P}^{\nu}$ –a.s. This implies in particular that for all $t\in[0,T]$ , $\Sigma_{t}$ should take values in $\mathbb{S}_{t}(X)$ , defined for all $x\in\Omega$ by

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{S}_{t}(x):=\big\{S\in\mathbb{S}_{+}^{d}\;:\;S=\big[\sigma\sigma^{\top}\big](t,x,u)\;\text{ for some }u\in U\big\}. $$

Furthermore, recall that the original set ${\cal U}$ of admissible controls is defined in Assumption A such that, for any control $\nu\in{\cal U}$ , there exists a unique weak solution to the controlled SDE (2.3). In particular, the set ${\cal U}^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ of admissible (constrained) controls also satisfies this property. Therefore, under the previous restriction that $\Sigma\in{\cal S}$ should be such that ${\cal U}^{\circ}(\Sigma)\neq\varnothing$ , it is clear that weak uniqueness also holds for SDE (3.3). In other words, for fixed $\Sigma\in{\cal S}$ , the weak solution $\widebar{\mathbb{P}}$ to SDE (3.3) defined in Remark 3.1 is actually unique, and therefore admits the predictable martingale representation property (see for example Jacod and Shiryaev (2003) [19, Theorem III.4.29]).

#### Remark 3.3.

This assumption that weak uniqueness holds for SDE (2.3), and thus for SDE (3.3), which is not enforced in [9], is considered here to avoid technical considerations regarding the martingale representation property. Indeed, without weak uniqueness, the solution $\widebar{\mathbb{P}}$ to SDE (3.3) may not admit the predictable martingale representation property. More precisely, the decomposition of any $(\mathbb{F},\widebar{\mathbb{P}})$ -local martingale with respect to $X$ would in general involve an extra martingale term, orthogonal to $X$ . As this martingale representation property is used to derive the optimal form of contracts, such an additional martingale term would complicate the study. In [9], this additional martingale term can be hidden in the component ‘ $K$ ’ of the solution $(Y,Z,K)$ to the appropriate second-order BSDE, as the set of probability measures considered is naturally saturated (see Possamaï, Tan, and Zhou (2018) [28, Definitions 5.1 and 5.2]). We refer back to Remark 2.2 for a discussion on the reasonableness of this assumption.

Again for future reference, we can summarise this alternative ‘first-best’ problem as follows.

#### Problem 3.

The ‘first-best’ reformulation of the original principal–agent problem is defined by

$$ \displaystyle V_{\rm P}^{\circ}:=\sup_{\Sigma\in{\cal S}}\sup_{\xi\in\Xi^{\circ}(\Sigma)}\sup_{\mathbb{P}^{\star}\in{\cal P}^{\circ,\star}(\xi,\Sigma)}J_{\rm P}(\xi,\mathbb{P}^{\star}), $$

where ${\cal P}^{\circ,\star}(\xi,\Sigma):=\{\mathbb{P}^{\star}\in{\cal P}^{\circ}(\Sigma)\;:\;V^{\circ}_{\rm A}(\xi,\Sigma)=J_{\rm A}(\xi,\mathbb{P}^{\star})\}\neq\varnothing$ for $\Sigma\in{\cal S}$ and $\xi\in\Xi^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ .

We first provide in Section 3.2 a very standard approach, relying on BSDEs theory, to characterise the optimal form of contracts for this ‘first-best’ alternative problem. The result is given in Theorem 3.9. We then prove the main result of this paper, namely Theorem 3.10, which states the equivalence between Problem 1 and Problem 3, i.e. $V_{\rm P}=V_{\rm P}^{\circ}$ . Before proceeding, one can already notice that the principal’s value $V_{\rm P}^{\circ}$ in the alternative ‘first-best’ problem summarised above, namely Problem 3, is greater than the value $V_{\rm P}$ in the original problem (Problem 1). This result is stated in the following Lemma 3.4, whose proof mostly relies on the observation that, in Problem 3, the principal has an additional control compared to the original problem.

#### Lemma 3.4.

The value of Problem 3 is greater than the value of Problem 1, i.e. $V_{\rm P}^{\circ}\geq V_{\rm P}$ .

Recall that we can assume, without loss of generality, that any potentially optimal contract $\xi\in\Xi$ for Problem 1 should be such that ${\cal P}^{\star}(\xi)\neq\varnothing$ , otherwise $V_{\rm P}=-\infty$ . One can thus consider $\mathbb{P}^{\star}\in{\cal P}^{\star}(\xi)$ , and its corresponding optimal effort process $\nu^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}}\in{\cal U}$ , leading to the following representation for the output process $X$ :

$$ \displaystyle X_{t}=x_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}\sigma\big(s,X,\nu^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}}_{s}\big)\big(\lambda\big(s,X,\nu^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}}_{s}\big)\mathrm{d}s+\mathrm{d}W_{s}\big),\;t\in[0,T],\;\mathbb{P}^{\star}\textnormal{--a.s.} $$

This naturally implies that the quadratic variation of $X$ , namely $\langle X\rangle$ , observable by the principal, satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\langle X\rangle_{t}=\int_{0}^{t}\Sigma^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}}_{s}\mathrm{d}s,\quad\text{where}\quad\Sigma^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}}_{t}:=\big[\sigma\sigma^{\top}\big]\big(t,X,\nu^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}}_{t}\big),\;t\in[0,T],\;\mathbb{P}^{\star}\textnormal{--a.s.}. $$

Note that the process $\Sigma^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}}$ defined above belongs to the set ${\cal S}$ by definition and we have $\nu^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}}\in{\cal U}^{\circ}(\Sigma^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}})$ , or equivalently, $\mathbb{P}^{\star}\in{\cal P}^{\circ}(\Sigma^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}})$ . Additionally, by definition of $\mathbb{P}^{\star}\in{\cal P}^{\star}(\xi)$ in (2.8), we have $V_{\rm A}(\xi)=J_{\rm A}(\xi,\mathbb{P}^{\star})\geq R_{\rm A}$ , and therefore

$$ \displaystyle R_{\rm A}\leq V_{\rm A}(\xi)=J_{\rm A}(\xi,\mathbb{P}^{\star})\leq\sup_{\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}^{\circ}(\Sigma^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}})}J_{\rm A}(\xi,\mathbb{P})=:V_{\rm A}^{\circ}\big(\xi,\Sigma^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}}\big), $$

implying in particular that $\xi\in\Xi^{\circ}(\Sigma^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}})$ . On the other hand, since we naturally have $V_{\rm A}(\xi)\geq V_{\rm A}^{\circ}(\xi,\Sigma)$ for all $\Sigma\in{\cal S}$ and $\xi\in\Xi$ , we can also deduce from the previous inequality that $\mathbb{P}^{\star}\in{\cal P}^{\circ,\star}(\xi,\Sigma^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}})$ . To summarise, for any $\xi\in\Xi$ and $\mathbb{P}^{\star}\in{\cal P}^{\star}(\xi)$ , there exists $\Sigma^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}}\in{\cal S}$ such that $\xi\in\Xi^{\circ}(\Sigma^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}})$ and $\mathbb{P}^{\star}\in{\cal P}^{\circ,\star}(\xi,\Sigma^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}})$ , which implies

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{\xi\in\Xi}\sup_{\mathbb{P}^{\star}\in{\cal P}^{\star}(\xi)}J_{\rm P}(\xi,\mathbb{P}^{\star})\leq\sup_{\Sigma\in{\cal S}}\sup_{\xi\in\Xi^{\circ}(\Sigma)}\sup_{\mathbb{P}^{\star}\in{\cal P}^{\circ,\star}(\xi,\Sigma)}J_{\rm P}(\xi,\mathbb{P}^{\star}) $$

and therefore concludes the proof. ∎

### 3.2 Solving the ‘first-best’ problem

While Problem 1 is proved to be equivalent to Problem 2 in [9] using the theory of 2BSDEs, we demonstrate in this section that the alternative ‘first-best’ problem, namely Problem 3 introduced above, can also be reformulated into a more standard stochastic control problem, defined as Problem 4 below, but relying on BSDEs only.

To be consistent with the approach developed in [9], we first introduce the appropriate Hamiltonian for the agent when the quadratic variation is fixed, as well as the relevant form of contracts for the reformulated problem (3.8). With this in mind, let $(t,x,y,z,S)\in[0,T]\times\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{S}^{d}_{+}$ , and consider the following Hamiltonian:

$$ \displaystyle{\cal H}^{\circ}_{\rm A}(t,x,y,z,S) \displaystyle:=\sup_{u\in U_{t}^{\circ}(x,S)}\;h^{\circ}_{\rm A}(t,x,y,z,u), \displaystyle\text{ with }\;h^{\circ}_{\rm A}(t,x,y,z,u) \displaystyle:=[\sigma\lambda](t,x,u)\cdot z-c_{\rm A}(t,x,u)-k_{\rm A}(t,x,u)y,\quad u\in U_{t}^{\circ}(x,S), $$

recalling that the set $U_{t}^{\circ}(x,S)$ is defined by (3.2).

#### Remark 3.5.

The Hamiltonian defined above in (3.11) is a simplified version of the original Hamiltonian in (2.10). Indeed, we consider here that the quadratic variation is fixed to some level through its density process $\Sigma$ , and in particular, cannot be optimised by the agent. In other words, at each time $t\in[0,T]$ , the agent has to choose his effort $\nu_{t}$ taking values in $U$ and satisfying $[\sigma\sigma^{\top}](t,X,\nu_{t})=\Sigma_{t}$ . Under this constraint, the ‘ $\gamma$ part’ of $h_{\rm A}$ defined in (2.10) becomes a constant, uncontrolled by the agent. Mathematically speaking, we have:

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{u\in U_{t}^{\circ}(x,S)}h_{\rm A}(t,x,y,z,\gamma,u) \displaystyle=\sup_{u\in U_{t}^{\circ}(x,S)}h^{\circ}_{\rm A}(t,x,y,z,u)+\dfrac{1}{2}{\rm Tr}\big[\gamma S\big]. $$

The previous equality also highlights the following relationship between the two Hamiltonians,

$$ \displaystyle{\cal H}_{\rm A}(t,x,y,z,\gamma) \displaystyle=\sup_{S\in\mathbb{S}_{t}(x)}\bigg\{{\cal H}^{\circ}_{\rm A}(t,x,y,z,S)+\dfrac{1}{2}{\rm Tr}\big[\gamma S\big]\bigg\}. $$

In other words, $2{\cal H}_{\rm A}(\cdot,\gamma)$ is the convex conjugate, or Legendre–Fenchel transformation, of $-2{\cal H}^{\circ}_{\rm A}(\cdot,S)$ .

In our reformulated problem, because the quadratic variation is originally fixed by the principal, the relevant form of contract will actually be similar to the one considered in principal–agent problems with drift control only. More precisely, we are led to consider here $\xi=Y_{T}^{y_{0},Z}$ , where the process $Y^{y_{0},Z}$ is defined as the solution to the following SDE,

$$ \displaystyle Y_{t}^{y_{0},Z}=y_{0}-\int_{0}^{t}{\cal H}_{\rm A}^{\circ}\big(s,X,Y^{y_{0},Z}_{s},Z_{s},\Sigma_{s}\big)\mathrm{d}s+\int_{0}^{t}Z_{s}\cdot\mathrm{d}X_{s},\quad\mathbb{P}\textnormal{--a.s.},\;\text{for all }\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}^{\circ}(\Sigma), $$

for a constant $y_{0}\in\mathbb{R}$ and a process $Z$ satisfying appropriate integrability conditions. In parallel with Definition 2.4, we define the set ${\cal V}^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ of appropriate processes $Z$ as follows.

#### Definition 3.6.

Let $y_{0}\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\Sigma\in{\cal S}$ . For any $\mathbb{F}$ –predictable processes $Z$ taking values in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , define the process $Y^{y_{0},Z}$ using (3.13). We will denote $Z\in{\cal V}^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ if moreover

- $(i)$ $\|Z\|^{p}_{\mathbb{H}^{p}}<\infty$ and $\|Y^{y_{0},Z}\|^{p}_{\mathbb{D}^{p}}<\infty$ for some $p>1;$

- $(ii)$ there exists $\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ such that $\displaystyle{\cal H}^{\circ}_{\rm A}\big(t,X,Y_{t}^{y_{0},Z},Z_{t},\Sigma_{t}\big)=h^{\circ}_{\rm A}\big(t,X,Y_{t}^{y_{0},Z},Z_{t},\nu_{t}^{\mathbb{P}}\big),\quad\mathrm{d}t\otimes\mathbb{P}\text{--a.e. on }[0,T]\times\Omega.$ (3.14)

For fixed $\Sigma\in{\cal S}$ , any contract defined by $\xi=Y_{T}^{y_{0},Z}$ through (3.13) for some $y_{0}\in\mathbb{R}$ and $Z\in{\cal V}^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ is an ${\cal F}_{T}$ -measurable random variable satisfying the integrability condition ( I p A ). If this contract satisfies in addition the agent’s participation constraint, we conclude that $\xi\in\Xi^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ . Conversely, we will prove below in Theorem 3.9 that the restriction to contracts of the form $\xi=Y_{T}^{y_{0},Z}$ , for $(y_{0},Z)\in[R_{\rm A},\infty)\times{\cal V}^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ , is without loss of generality.

#### Remark 3.7.

Intuitively, when the density $\Sigma\in{\cal S}$ of the quadratic variation is fixed, the new form of contracts (3.13) can be derived from the general form of contracts (2.11). Indeed, starting from (2.11) under $\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ , and using in particular Remark 3.5 on the Hamiltonian, we derive the following representation,

$$ \displaystyle Y_{t}^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma} \displaystyle=y_{0}-\int_{0}^{t}\bigg({\cal H}^{\circ}_{\rm A}\big(s,X,Y^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma}_{s},Z_{s},\Sigma_{s}\big)+\dfrac{1}{2}{\rm Tr}\big[\Gamma_{s}\Sigma_{s}\big]\bigg)\mathrm{d}s+\int_{0}^{t}Z_{s}\cdot\mathrm{d}X_{s}+\dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{t}{\rm Tr}\big[\Gamma_{s}\Sigma_{s}\big]\mathrm{d}s,\;t\in[0,T], $$

thus naturally leading to (3.13), since the part of the contract indexed by $\Gamma$ simplifies.

Before stating the main result of this section, we first solve the agent’s problem (3.6), in order to confirm the intuition on the relevant contract form (3.13) highlighted by the previous remark. The proof of this result only relies on the theory of BSDEs, as opposed to 2BSDEs, needed to characterise the agent’s problem originally defined in (2.5) (see [9, Proposition 4.6]).

#### Proposition 3.8.

Let $\Sigma\in{\cal S}$ and $\xi\in\Xi^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ . There exist a unique ${\cal F}_{0}^{\widebar{\mathbb{P}}+}$ -measurable random variable $Y_{0}$ , satisfying $\mathbb{E}^{\widebar{\mathbb{P}}}\left[Y_{0}\right]\geq R_{\rm A}$ , and a unique $Z\in\mathbb{H}^{p}$ such that $\xi=Y_{T}$ , for $Y\in\mathbb{D}^{p}$ defined as the solution to the following SDE:

$$ \displaystyle Y_{t}=Y_{0}-\int_{0}^{t}{\cal H}_{\rm A}^{\circ}\big(s,X,Y_{s},Z_{s},\Sigma_{s}\big)\mathrm{d}s+\int_{0}^{t}Z_{s}\cdot\mathrm{d}X_{s},\;t\in[0,T],\;\widebar{\mathbb{P}}\textnormal{--a.s.} $$

Moreover,

- $(i)$ $V_{\rm A}^{\circ}(\xi,\Sigma)=\mathbb{E}^{\widebar{\mathbb{P}}}\left[Y_{0}\right]\geq R_{\rm A};$

- $(ii)$ $\mathbb{P}^{\circ}\in{\cal P}^{\circ,\star}(\xi,\Sigma)$ if and only if ${\cal H}^{\circ}_{\rm A}(t,X,Y_{t},Z_{t},\Sigma_{t})=h^{\circ}_{\rm A}(t,X,Y_{t},Z_{t},\nu_{t}^{\mathbb{P}^{\circ}})$ , $\mathrm{d}t\otimes\mathbb{P}^{\circ}\text{--a.e. on }[0,T]\times\Omega$ .

Step 1. We fix $\Sigma\in{\cal S}$ and $\xi\in\Xi^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ to consider the following BSDE

$$ \displaystyle Y_{t}=\xi+\int_{t}^{T}{\cal H}_{\rm A}^{\circ}\big(s,X,Y_{s},Z_{s},\Sigma_{s}\big)\mathrm{d}s-\int_{t}^{T}Z_{s}\cdot\mathrm{d}X_{s},\quad t\in[0,T]\quad\widebar{\mathbb{P}}\textnormal{--a.s.}, $$

and argue that there exists a unique solution $(Y,Z)\in\mathbb{D}^{p}\times\mathbb{H}^{p}$ for some $p>1$ , to deduce (3.15). For this, we let $p_{1}>1$ and $p_{2}>1$ such that (2.6) and Condition I p A hold, respectively. For all $p^{\prime}\in(1,p_{1})$ , using Jensen’s inequality and changing the probability from $\widebar{\mathbb{P}}$ to $\mathbb{P}^{\nu}$ using $M^{\nu}$ defined in (3.5), we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{\widebar{\mathbb{P}}}\Bigg[\bigg(\int_{0}^{T}\big|{\cal H}^{\circ}_{\rm A}(t,X,0,0,\Sigma_{t})\big|\mathrm{d}t\bigg)^{p^{\prime}}\Bigg] \displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}^{\widebar{\mathbb{P}}}\bigg[\int_{0}^{T}\big|{\cal H}^{\circ}_{\rm A}(t,X,0,0,\Sigma_{t})\big|^{p^{\prime}}\mathrm{d}t\bigg]=\mathbb{E}^{\widebar{\mathbb{P}}}\bigg[\int_{0}^{T}\inf_{u\in U^{\circ}(\Sigma)}\big|c_{\rm A}(t,X,u)\big|^{p^{\prime}}\mathrm{d}t\bigg] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}^{\nu}}\bigg[M_{T}^{\nu}\int_{0}^{T}\inf_{u\in U^{\circ}(\Sigma)}\big|c_{\rm A}(t,X,u)\big|^{p^{\prime}}\mathrm{d}t\bigg] \displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}^{\nu}}\Bigg[\bigg(\int_{0}^{T}\inf_{u\in U^{\circ}(\Sigma)}\big|c_{\rm A}(t,X,u)\big|^{p^{\prime}}\mathrm{d}t\bigg)^{q_{1}}\Bigg]^{\frac{1}{q_{1}}}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}^{\nu}}\Big[\big|M_{T}^{\nu}\big|^{q_{2}}\Big]^{\frac{1}{q_{2}}}, $$

where the last inequality comes from Holder’s inequality with $q_{1}:=p_{1}/p^{\prime}>1$ and $q_{2}>1$ its Holder’s conjugate, i.e. such that $\frac{1}{q_{1}}+\frac{1}{q_{2}}=1$ . Since $\lambda$ is bounded, there exists a constant $C>0$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{\widebar{\mathbb{P}}}\Bigg[\bigg(\int_{0}^{T}\big|{\cal H}^{\circ}_{\rm A}(t,X,0,0,\Sigma_{t})\big|\mathrm{d}t\bigg)^{p^{\prime}}\Bigg] \displaystyle\leq C\;\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}^{\nu}}\bigg[\int_{0}^{T}\inf_{u\in U^{\circ}(\Sigma)}\big|c_{\rm A}(t,X,u)\big|^{p_{1}}\mathrm{d}t\bigg]^{\frac{1}{q_{1}}}\leq C\sup_{\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}\bigg[\int_{0}^{T}\big|c_{\rm A}(t,X,\nu_{t})\big|^{p_{1}}\mathrm{d}t\bigg]^{\frac{1}{q_{1}}}, $$

which is finite since (2.6) holds for $p_{1}>1$ . By similar arguments, we deduce from the fact that Condition I p A is satisfied for $p_{2}>1$ that $\mathbb{E}^{\widebar{\mathbb{P}}}[|\xi|^{p^{\prime\prime}}]<+\infty$ , for $p^{\prime\prime}\in(1,p_{2})$ . We thus obtain the following integrability condition,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{\widebar{\mathbb{P}}}\bigg[|\xi|^{p}+\bigg(\int_{0}^{T}\big|{\cal H}^{\circ}_{\rm A}(t,X,0,0,\Sigma_{t})\big|\mathrm{d}t\bigg)^{p}\bigg]<\infty,\quad p\in(1,p_{1}\wedge p_{2}). $$

Finally, by the boundedness of $\sigma,\lambda$ and $k_{\rm A}$ , the Hamiltonian ${\cal H}_{\rm A}^{\circ}$ is uniformly Lipschitz-continuous in $(y,z)$ . Since the assumptions of Briand, Delyon, Hu, Pardoux, and Stoica (2003) [6, Theorem 4.2] are satisfied (see also Bouchard, Possamaï, Tan, and Zhou (2018) [5, Theorem 4.1] for a more recent result), and $\widebar{\mathbb{P}}$ satisfies the predictable martingale representation property, we deduce that there exists a unique solution $(Y,Z)\in\mathbb{D}^{p}\times\mathbb{H}^{p}$ to BSDE (3.16), for some $p>1$ . In particular, such solution satisfies Definition 3.6 $(i)$ and $Y_{0}$ is a ${\cal F}_{0}^{\widebar{\mathbb{P}}+}$ -measurable random variable.

Step 2. We now prove the equality $(i)$ , namely $V^{\circ}_{\rm A}(\xi,\Sigma)=\mathbb{E}^{\widebar{\mathbb{P}}}[Y_{0}]$ . As a direct consequence, we will obtain that $Z\in\mathbb{H}^{p}$ , introduced in Step 1, satisfies (3.14) in Definition 3.6, implying that $(ii)$ is verified. By Step 1, any contract $\xi\in\Xi^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ can be written as

$$ \displaystyle\xi=Y_{T}:=Y_{0}-\int_{0}^{T}{\cal H}_{\rm A}^{\circ}\big(s,X,Y_{s},Z_{s},\Sigma_{s}\big)\mathrm{d}s+\int_{0}^{T}Z_{s}\cdot\mathrm{d}X_{s},\quad\widebar{\mathbb{P}}\textnormal{--a.s.} $$

Writing the dynamics under some arbitrary admissible effort $\nu\in{\cal U}^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ , i.e. under $\mathbb{P}^{\nu}\in{\cal P}^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ , we have:

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}Y_{t}=\big(-{\cal H}_{\rm A}^{\circ}\big(t,X,Y_{t},Z_{t},\Sigma_{t}\big)+Z_{t}\cdot[\sigma\lambda](t,X,\nu_{t})\big)\mathrm{d}t+Z_{t}\cdot\sigma(t,X,\nu_{t})\mathrm{d}W_{t},\quad\mathbb{P}^{\nu}\textnormal{--a.s.} $$

Applying Ito’s formula and using the definition of $h^{\circ}_{\rm A}$ , one can compute, still under $\mathbb{P}^{\nu}\in{\cal P}^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle{\cal K}^{\mathbb{P}^{\nu}}_{\rm A}(T)Y_{T}-\int_{0}^{T}{\cal K}^{\mathbb{P}^{\nu}}_{\rm A}(t)c_{\rm A}(t,X,\nu_{t})\mathrm{d}t=Y_{0} \displaystyle-\int_{0}^{T}{\cal K}^{\mathbb{P}^{\nu}}_{\rm A}(t)\big({\cal H}^{\circ}_{\rm A}(t,X,Y_{t},Z_{t},\Sigma_{t})-h^{\circ}_{\rm A}(t,X,Y_{t},Z_{t},\nu_{t})\big)\mathrm{d}t \displaystyle+\int_{0}^{T}{\cal K}^{\mathbb{P}^{\nu}}_{\rm A}(t)Z_{t}\cdot\sigma(t,X,\nu_{t})\mathrm{d}W_{t}. $$

Using this representation in the agent’s objective function, and noticing that, since $Z\in\mathbb{H}^{p}$ and $k_{\rm A},\sigma$ are bounded, the expectation of the stochastic integral term vanishes, we obtain:
